abstract: Background Although 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (HPGD) is known to regulate the metabolism of prostaglandins and lipoxin A4, and its dysregulation has been implicated in various cancers, its role in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) has not been determined. This study is the first to comprehensively characterize HPGD expression in ESCC and establish its clinical relevance in predicting patient outcomes. Furthermore, we elucidated the previously unrecognized molecular mechanisms through which HPGD suppresses ESCC progression and its potential as a novel therapeutic target. Methods Transcriptome sequencing was performed on paired tumor and adjacent normal tissues from deceased patients with ESCC to identify differentially expressed genes. The differential expression of the HPGD gene was subsequently validated in two independent, large-scale ESCC patient cohorts, and its prognostic significance was evaluated. To evaluate the functional role of HPGD in ESCC, the enzyme was overexpressed in ESCC cell lines, and a series of in vitro assays were conducted to assess its effects on proliferation, apoptosis, invasion, and migration. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of HPGD, we performed transcriptomic sequencing to profile gene expression changes in ESCC cells. Through multiple analyses, including measurements of lipid peroxidation, intracellular ferrous ion and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, dual-fluorescence flow cytometry for autophagy, phosphoprotein microarrays, biotin pull-down assays, and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), we demonstrated that HPGD regulates the malignant phenotype of ESCC cells primarily by inducing ferroptosis and autophagy. Finally, the impact of HPGD on ESCC tumor growth was validated in vivo using a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice. Results HPGD expression was significantly lower in ESCC tissues than in normal tissues and was negatively correlated with tumor cell differentiation and patient outcomes. HPGD overexpression inhibited ESCC cell proliferation, invasion, and migration in vitro and in xenograft tumor growth in vivo. In vitro experiments demonstrated that HPGD suppresses ERK1/2 activation by facilitating lipoxin A4 (LXA4) degradation. This inhibition facilitates binding of the RNA-binding protein U2AF2 to the promoter region of the transferrin receptor (TFRC), thereby increasing TFRC expression. Consequently, these alterations lead to intracellular iron accumulation and initiate ferroptosis. Excessive generation of ROS during ferroptosis results in hyperactivation of autophagy via the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway. Mitigating the HPGD-induced upregulation of TFRC or reducing ROS production effectively reverses ferroptosis, prevents excessive autophagy, and ameliorates malignant cell phenotypes. Conclusions HPGD exerts its antitumor effects by promoting ferroptosis through the LXA4-ERK1/2-U2AF2 signaling axis, which in turn induces autophagy hyperactivation via the AMPK-mTOR pathway. These findings suggest that HPGD is a promising therapeutic target for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and reveal the nonclassic role of the RNA-binding protein U2AF2 in regulating the expression of TFRC by acting like a transcription factor. Materials and methods
Human tissue samples
Human esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) tissues and matched normal tissues were obtained from two ESCC cohorts at the Affiliated Huai’an First People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Cohort 1 consisted of 147 patients who underwent radical esophagectomy between 2013 and 2017, and Cohort 2 consisted of 119 patients who underwent the same procedure between 2016 and 2017 at the Thoracic Surgery Department of the same hospital. Samples from Cohort 1 were used for total RNA extraction to validate gene mRNA expression levels, whereas samples from Cohort 2 were utilized for the construction of tissue microarrays to assess protein expression levels through immunohistochemistry (IHC). All samples were collected and stored in the Esophageal Cancer Biobank under HIPAA guidelines, with sample collection supervised by the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Huai’an First People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. All patients were pathologically diagnosed with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma via endoscopic biopsy before surgery, informed about the study, and provided informed consent before inclusion. TNM staging was performed in accordance of the TNM classification system of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC). Samples from Cohort 1 were used for RNA-seq and mRNA expression validation, while those from Cohort 2 were used for tissue microarray preparation and protein extraction. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Huai’an No.1 People’s Hospital, Nanjing Medical University (KY-2023-054-01).
RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)
Total RNA was extracted by RNeasy Kits for RNA Purification purchased from Qiagen. mRNA was isolated using oligo magnetic beads and processed into small fragments for cDNA synthesis. Libraries were generated using the NEBNext Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) for the Illumina system according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequencing was conducted using the Illumina HiSeq XTEN platform.
Transient transfection and establishment of stable cell lines
KYSE30 and KYSE150 cells were seeded into a 6-well plate and transfected with pl/HPGD or a plRES2 negative control plasmid using the Lipofectamine™ 3000 protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). After G418 selection, the cells were collected, and total protein was extracted to assess the HPGD expression levels via Western blotting.
Plasmid construction and dual luciferase reporter gene analysis
The HPGD gene was amplified by PCR and inserted into the plRES2 vector; the results were subsequently verified by sequencing. The constructed plasmid vectors and primers are shown in Supplementary Table (1) The human TFRC promoter sequence from − 2000 to + 100 bp relative to the transcriptional start site was obtained from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI,
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
). The fragments were inserted into the pGL3-Basic vector (Promega, USA), which was renamed pGL3-TFRC-FL. Following the molecular docking analysis, the binding site of U2AF2 within the TFRC promoter region was mutated, and the resulting mutated fragment was subsequently cloned into the pGL3-Basic vector. All plasmids were constructed by the GENERAL BIOL company (An Hui, China). The constructed plasmid vectors and sequences are shown in Supplementary Table (2) Transfection and dual-luciferase reporter assays were performed following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Cell culture
Normal human esophageal epithelial cells (HEECs) and cells from an ESCC cancer cell line (KYSE30) were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (10% FBS) and 1% penicillin‒streptomycin mix (1% PS). The cells from the tumor-derived ESCC cancer cell line KYSE150 were cultured in high-glucose DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (10% FBS) and 1% penicillin‒streptomycin mix (1% PS). All the cell Lines were grown in an incubator at 37 °C with 90% humidity and 5% CO₂.
Real-time quantitative PCR
RNA from tissue samples or cells was extracted using TRIzol, and the RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using the Prime Script RT Master Mix kit. RT‒qPCR experiments were performed using a fluorescent quantitative PCR kit in an ABI StepOnePlus™ real-time PCR system, with GAPDH as the internal control. The primer sequences are shown in Supplementary Table 3. The results were reported using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method.
Construction of small interfering RNAs
siTFRC and negative control siRNAs were synthesized by Proteinbio (China). The siRNA interference sequences are Listed in Supplementary Table 3. Cells were transfected with the siRNAs using Lipofectamine™ 3000 according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA was extracted 24 h post-transfection, and total protein was collected at 48 h. The efficiency of gene silencing was evaluated by qPCR and Western blot analyses. The siRNA sequences are detailed in Supplementary Table 4.
Immunoblotting
Tissues were processed using a DHS Q24R tissue homogenizer and lysed with RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with PMSF protease inhibitor. The protein concentration was measured using a BCA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The samples were mixed with 5× protein loading Buffer and denatured by boiling at 100 °C. Proteins were separated by SDS‒PAGE, transferred onto PVDF membranes, and blocked with 5% BSA. The membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by washing and incubation with secondary antibodies (Cell Signaling Technology, USA) at room temperature for 1 h. After a final wash, the protein bands were visualized using enhanced ECL reagent (Proteinbio, China).
Flow cytometric analysis
For cell cycle analysis, ESCC cells were collected and adjusted to a concentration of 1 × 10⁶ cells/mL. A 1 mL aliquot of the single-cell suspension was centrifuged, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was fixed in 70% cold ethanol overnight at 4 °C. The following day, the cells were stained with PI/RNase A solution (KeyGEN BioTECH, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. The cell cycle distribution was then analyzed using a CytoFLEX SRT flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, USA). For apoptosis detection, the cells were collected following EDTA-free gentle trypsin treatment for 1 min, after which the digestion was immediately quenched using medium supplemented with 10% FBS. Afterward, the cells were washed with precooled PBS. Annexin V-FITC Reagent and PI Reagent (Elabscience, China) were added, and the samples were incubated at room temperature in the dark for 15 min and analyzed with a CytoFLEX SRT flow cytometer.

ESCC cells were digested with trypsin, resuspended in serum-free medium, and counted. The cell concentration was adjusted to 5 × 10⁴ cells/mL, and 200 µL of the suspension was added to the upper chamber of a Transwell insert. The lower chamber of a 24-well plate was filled with 600 µL of medium containing 10% FBS as a chemoattractant. After 48 h of incubation, nonmigrated cells on the upper surface were gently removed with a cotton swab. The membranes were fixed with methanol and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. The migrated cells were counted in five randomly selected fields under a phase-contrast microscope at 10× magnification. For the invasion assay, the upper chamber was precoated with Matrigel, and the same procedure was followed.
RTCA
After 50 µl of medium was added to each well of an E-Plate 16, the baseline data were recorded. Transiently transfected ESCC cells were collected, counted, and resuspended at a concentration of 5 × 10⁴ cells/mL. Afterward, 100 µl of the well-mixed cell suspension was added to each well, and the contents were incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The E-Plate 16 was transferred to the xCELLigence RTCA instrument and placed in an incubator for real-time dynamic monitoring of cell proliferation.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis
ESCC tissue samples were fixed in 10% formalin, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. After deparaffinization and rehydration, the samples were subject to Heat-induced antigen retrieval. The sections were then blocked with 10% BSA at 37 °C for 1 h, followed by three washes with PBS. The primary antibody was applied, and the slides were incubated overnight at 4 °C. After the cells were washed with PBS, the secondary antibody was added, and the samples were incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Following the washes, color was developed using DAB, and the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin. Images were captured and analyzed under a microscope.
Clonogenic and soft agar assays
Three hundred cells were seeded in a 12-well plate and incubated for 2 weeks. Cell colonies were fixed with 4% PFA, stained with 0.1% crystal violet, imaged and then manually counted. Soft agar assays were performed as previously described [
23
]. After 20 days of culture, the tumor cell colonies were imaged and counted. The size of 25 randomly selected colonies per well was measured and calculated using the formula (length + width)/2.

A biotin-labeled DNA fragment containing the TFRC promoter sequence was generated via PCR. The resulting biotin-tagged cDNA construct was transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine™ 3000 (Lipo3000) following the manufacturer’s protocol. After 48 h, the transfected cells were harvested and lysed under gentle conditions to preserve protein‒DNA interactions. The cell lysates were incubated with streptavidin-conjugated magnetic beads to specifically capture the biotinylated TFRC promoter complexes. After thorough washing to remove nonspecific binders, the bound protein‒DNA complexes were eluted. The eluted proteins were then separated via SDS‒PAGE, and the gel was stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue. Protein bands of interest showing differential expression or enrichment were excised from the gel and subjected to in-gel digestion. Purified proteins from the streptavidin pull-down were analyzed with liquid chromatography‒tandem mass spectrometry (LC‒MS/MS). Both data-dependent acquisition (DDA) and data-independent acquisition (DIA) methods were employed. Raw DDA data were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer 2.2 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), while DIA data were processed with Spectronaut software (version 9.0; Biognosys). Quantitative and statistical analyses were conducted within the R statistical environment to identify and validate protein interactors.
Ferrous ion assay
The cells were subsequently washed with PBS, digested, collected, and lysed on ice for 10 min. Following centrifugation at 15,000 × g for 10 min, the supernatant was collected and used for ferrous ion detection according to the protocol of the Cell Ferrous Iron Colorimetric Assay Kit (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
ROS detection assay
ESCC cells were harvested and resuspended in serum-free medium containing 10 µM of the fluorescent probe DCFH-DA (Nanjing Jiancheng, China). The cells were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark to allow intracellular uptake and conversion of DCFH-DA to its fluorescent form upon reaction with the ROS. After incubation, the cells were washed to remove excess probe, resuspended in fresh medium, and immediately analyzed via flow cytometry to quantify intracellular ROS levels on the basis of fluorescence intensity.
Autophagy assay
Cells that stably overexpressed the SensGFP-StubRFP-LC3 autophagy reporter were transfected with siRNA targeting TFRC (siTFRC). Twenty-four hours after transfection, the cells were treated with rapamycin (MedChemExpress, USA) to induce autophagy. After an additional 24 h of incubation, the cell nuclei were stained with DAPI to visualize the nuclear morphology. Fluorescence images were then captured using a laser scanning confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan), and signals were collected in the SensGFP, StubRFP, and DAPI channels to assess autophagic flux and nuclear staining.
Fluorescence detection of lipid peroxidation in cells and mitochondria
ESCC cells were seeded onto coverslips, placed in a 24-well plate, and allowed to adhere overnight. The cells were treated with ferrostatin-1 (MedChemExpress, USA) for 24 h. Mito-Tracker Green (Proteinbio, China) was subsequently added, and the samples were incubated for 30 min to ensure labelling of the mitochondria. After two washes with HBSS, the cells were stained with MitoSOX Red (MedChemExpress, USA) for an additional 30 min to detect mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. Finally, the nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and the cells were imaged using a laser scanning confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan).
Lipid hydroperoxide (MDA) and LPO detection assays
For the MDA assay, cells were homogenized in 303 µL of lysis solution on ice. The lysates were sonicated to shear the DNA and reduce viscosity and then centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 10 min to remove insoluble debris. The resulting supernatant was collected and used for MDA measurement following the instructions provided in the Lipid Peroxidation (MDA) Assay Kit (Abcam Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
For the LPO assay, cells were sonicated in HPLC-grade water or metal ion-free media to avoid interference from transition metals. The supernatants were immediately collected after sonication and processed with a Lipid Hydroperoxide (LPO) Assay Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Abcam Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).

Cells were treated with or without TFRC siRNA for 48 h. The culture medium and cells were collected for ELISA and GPX4 activity assays. GSH and LXA4 ELISA kits (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) were used to measure the levels of GSH and LXA4, respectively, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A Glutathione Peroxidase 4 Activity Assay Kit (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) was used to measure the activity of GPX4 according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
ChIP analysis was performed according to the instructions of the ChIP Assay Kit (56383; Cell Signaling Technology, America). Cells were cultured in 6-well plates with or without EGF for 48 h and then fixed via the addition of 16% formaldehyde directly to the culture medium. After 10 min of fixation at room temperature, the medium was supplemented with glycine to halt fixation. Chromatin was fragmented to 200–400 bp in 20 cycles (30 s on, 30 s off cycles, High Setting) of sonication. Chromatin immunoprecipitation was conducted overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against U2AF2 (Proteintech, America) and 2 µl of normal rabbit IgG (provided in the ChIP Assay Kit). After reverse cross-linking and DNA extraction, the immunoprecipitated chromatin was used as the template for RT‒PCR analysis. The primers used to detect the promoter of TFRC are Listed in Supplemental Table 3.
Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)
FISH experiments were performed as follows: 6-well plates were seeded at a density of 5 × 10
5
cells/well, and serum-free basal medium was used for overnight starvation. The cells were subsequently stimulated with EGF (100 ng/ml) for 30 min, followed by the addition of 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 30 min. The cells were then permeabilized at room temperature using Proteinase K (10 µg/ml) for 5 minutes. To reduce the background signal, the cells were incubated with HCl (0.5 M) and acetylation solution at room temperature for 10 min. A hybridization solution containing the probes was hybridized overnight with the cells at 24–65 °C in the dark. Finally, DAPI (5 µg/ml) was added to stain the cell nuclei. The sequences of the FISH-labeled oligonucleotide probes are provided in Supplementary Table 4. The following steps were performed as described in the Immunofluorescence Staining protocol for the IF experiments above.
In vivo xenograft experiments
Four-week-old nude mice were purchased from Nanjing Senbao Biological Products Center. KYSE150 and KYSE30 cells stably transfected with plasmid plRES2 that expressing HPGD were subcutaneously injected into the armpits of the mice. Tumor size and survival rate were measured every 7 days. On day 28, five mice from each group were euthanized, and tumor tissues were harvested for ROS, ferrous ion, GPx4, GSH, MDA, LPO, and LXA4 measurement using corresponding detection kits. The survival time of each group of mice was recorded in a duplicate experiment. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Huai’an No. 1 People’s Hospital and was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the National Animal Care and Ethics Institution on March 21, 2024 (DW-P-2024-015-01).
Statistical analysis
Clinical sample data analysis was conducted using SPSS 20.0 software. In vitro and in vivo experimental data were plotted using GraphPad Prism software. Survival curves were estimated via Kaplan‒Meier analysis and compared with the log-rank test. All the results were confirmed in at least three independent experiments; Student’s t tests were used for between-group comparisons of the means of quantitative data, and a
P
value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

In vivo xenograft experiments
Four-week-old nude mice were purchased from Nanjing Senbao Biological Products Center. Introduction
Esophageal cancer is among the most common cancers affecting the digestive system, ranking seventh in incidence and sixth in mortality among cancers worldwide. More than half of all cases occur in China, all of which are predominantly squamous cell carcinomas [
1
]. Patients who are diagnosed early with localized ESCC tend to have better outcomes when they undergo minimally invasive procedures such as endoscopic mucosal resection or endoscopic submucosal dissection [
2
,
3
]. However, patients typically present with symptoms only after the disease has progressed to the middle or late stages, which are characterized by regional lymph node or adjacent organ metastasis [
4
], resulting in a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30% [
5
]. The long-term efficacy of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined with surgery for esophageal cancer is a subject of ongoing debate [
3
,
6
,
7
]. Although neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined with immunotherapy has shown promising short-term results in patients with advanced ESCC, improvements in long-term survival have been limited [
8
]. Recent research involving integrative bioinformatics methodologies, such as exome sequencing [
9
,
10
], proteomics [
11
], single-cell sequencing [
12
], and tumor-infiltrated immune cell and immune marker analysis [
13
], has focused on various stages of cancer in identifying novel diagnostic and therapeutic targets. However, the mechanisms underlying ESCC development remain unclear.
Transcriptomic analysis of tissue samples from an ESCC cohort revealed that 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (HPGD) expression was significantly lower in ESCC. HPGD converts the hydroxyl groups of prostaglandins into inactive ketone metabolites and reduces prostaglandin levels and activities [
14
]. HPGD modulates the function of regulatory T (Treg) cells to maintain adipose tissue homeostasis and prevent local inflammation and systemic insulin resistance [
15
]. This enzyme also plays important roles in muscle aging and tissue regeneration [
14
,
16
]. In gastric cancer, HPGD promotes antitumor immunity by regulating FOXP3
+
Treg cells [
17
], and single-nucleotide polymorphisms in HPGD are closely associated with the risk of developing colorectal and prostate cancers [
18
,
19
]. Numerous studies have shown that HPGD suppresses tumor growth through various signaling pathways by inhibiting PGE2 synthesis in different cancers. For example, HPGD inhibits pancreatic cancer development through FGF1 and ALDH1 signaling [
20
,
21
] and liver cancer growth via PPARγ-mediated activation of the p21-WAF1-Cip1 signaling axis and suppresses stemness and progression in cholangiocarcinoma by inhibiting PTGER1 [
22
]. In colorectal cancer, HPGD expression is closely associated with the development of inflammation-driven cancers [
23
]. Nevertheless, the details of the mechanisms through which HPGD inhibits tumor progression remain unclear, particularly in ESCC, where its relationship with patient clinicopathology and functional roles in ESCC have not been elucidated.
In this study, we examined the role played by HPGD in ESCC. Validation in clinical cohort samples demonstrated that reduced HPGD expression was associated with poor tumor cell differentiation and an unfavorable outcome for ESCC patients. Overexpression of HPGD in ESCC cells markedly inhibited cell proliferation, invasion, and migration. Notably, our research revealed that HPGD facilitates the atypical binding of the RNA-binding protein U2AF2 to the DNA promoter region of TFRC via the LXA4-ERK1/2 pathway, thereby modulating TFRC expression. This mechanism not only induces ferroptosis in ESCC but also activates autophagy through the AMPK–mTOR pathway, effectively limiting ESCC progression. These findings were corroborated in vivo using a nude mouse xenograft model, in which we demonstrated that HPGD significantly suppresses tumor growth.

Raw DDA data were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer 2.2 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), while DIA data were processed with Spectronaut software (version 9.0; Biognosys). Quantitative and statistical analyses were conducted within the R statistical environment to identify and validate protein interactors.
Ferrous ion assay
The cells were subsequently washed with PBS, digested, collected, and lysed on ice for 10 min. Following centrifugation at 15,000 × g for 10 min, the supernatant was collected and used for ferrous ion detection according to the protocol of the Cell Ferrous Iron Colorimetric Assay Kit (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
ROS detection assay
ESCC cells were harvested and resuspended in serum-free medium containing 10 µM of the fluorescent probe DCFH-DA (Nanjing Jiancheng, China). The cells were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark to allow intracellular uptake and conversion of DCFH-DA to its fluorescent form upon reaction with the ROS. After incubation, the cells were washed to remove excess probe, resuspended in fresh medium, and immediately analyzed via flow cytometry to quantify intracellular ROS levels on the basis of fluorescence intensity.
Autophagy assay
Cells that stably overexpressed the SensGFP-StubRFP-LC3 autophagy reporter were transfected with siRNA targeting TFRC (siTFRC). Twenty-four hours after transfection, the cells were treated with rapamycin (MedChemExpress, USA) to induce autophagy. After an additional 24 h of incubation, the cell nuclei were stained with DAPI to visualize the nuclear morphology. Fluorescence images were then captured using a laser scanning confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan), and signals were collected in the SensGFP, StubRFP, and DAPI channels to assess autophagic flux and nuclear staining.
Fluorescence detection of lipid peroxidation in cells and mitochondria
ESCC cells were seeded onto coverslips, placed in a 24-well plate, and allowed to adhere overnight. The cells were treated with ferrostatin-1 (MedChemExpress, USA) for 24 h. Mito-Tracker Green (Proteinbio, China) was subsequently added, and the samples were incubated for 30 min to ensure labelling of the mitochondria. After two washes with HBSS, the cells were stained with MitoSOX Red (MedChemExpress, USA) for an additional 30 min to detect mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. Finally, the nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and the cells were imaged using a laser scanning confocal microscope (Nikon, Japan).
Lipid hydroperoxide (MDA) and LPO detection assays
For the MDA assay, cells were homogenized in 303 µL of lysis solution on ice. The lysates were sonicated to shear the DNA and reduce viscosity and then centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 10 min to remove insoluble debris. The resulting supernatant was collected and used for MDA measurement following the instructions provided in the Lipid Peroxidation (MDA) Assay Kit (Abcam Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
For the LPO assay, cells were sonicated in HPLC-grade water or metal ion-free media to avoid interference from transition metals. The supernatants were immediately collected after sonication and processed with a Lipid Hydroperoxide (LPO) Assay Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Abcam Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
ELISA and GPX4 activity assays
Cells were treated with or without TFRC siRNA for 48 h. The culture medium and cells were collected for ELISA and GPX4 activity assays. GSH and LXA4 ELISA kits (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) were used to measure the levels of GSH and LXA4, respectively, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A Glutathione Peroxidase 4 Activity Assay Kit (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) was used to measure the activity of GPX4 according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
ChIP analysis was performed according to the instructions of the ChIP Assay Kit (56383; Cell Signaling Technology, America). Cells were cultured in 6-well plates with or without EGF for 48 h and then fixed via the addition of 16% formaldehyde directly to the culture medium. After 10 min of fixation at room temperature, the medium was supplemented with glycine to halt fixation. Chromatin was fragmented to 200–400 bp in 20 cycles (30 s on, 30 s off cycles, High Setting) of sonication. Chromatin immunoprecipitation was conducted overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against U2AF2 (Proteintech, America) and 2 µl of normal rabbit IgG (provided in the ChIP Assay Kit). After reverse cross-linking and DNA extraction, the immunoprecipitated chromatin was used as the template for RT‒PCR analysis. The primers used to detect the promoter of TFRC are Listed in Supplemental Table 3.
Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)
FISH experiments were performed as follows: 6-well plates were seeded at a density of 5 × 10
5
cells/well, and serum-free basal medium was used for overnight starvation. The cells were subsequently stimulated with EGF (100 ng/ml) for 30 min, followed by the addition of 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 30 min. The cells were then permeabilized at room temperature using Proteinase K (10 µg/ml) for 5 minutes. To reduce the background signal, the cells were incubated with HCl (0.5 M) and acetylation solution at room temperature for 10 min. A hybridization solution containing the probes was hybridized overnight with the cells at 24–65 °C in the dark. Finally, DAPI (5 µg/ml) was added to stain the cell nuclei. The sequences of the FISH-labeled oligonucleotide probes are provided in Supplementary Table 4. The following steps were performed as described in the Immunofluorescence Staining protocol for the IF experiments above.
In vivo xenograft experiments
Four-week-old nude mice were purchased from Nanjing Senbao Biological Products Center. KYSE150 and KYSE30 cells stably transfected with plasmid plRES2 that expressing HPGD were subcutaneously injected into the armpits of the mice. Tumor size and survival rate were measured every 7 days. On day 28, five mice from each group were euthanized, and tumor tissues were harvested for ROS, ferrous ion, GPx4, GSH, MDA, LPO, and LXA4 measurement using corresponding detection kits. The survival time of each group of mice was recorded in a duplicate experiment. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Huai’an No. 1 People’s Hospital and was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the National Animal Care and Ethics Institution on March 21, 2024 (DW-P-2024-015-01).
Statistical analysis
Clinical sample data analysis was conducted using SPSS 20.0 software. In vitro and in vivo experimental data were plotted using GraphPad Prism software. Survival curves were estimated via Kaplan‒Meier analysis and compared with the log-rank test. All the results were confirmed in at least three independent experiments; Student’s t tests were used for between-group comparisons of the means of quantitative data, and a
P
value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

We collected postoperative tumor tissues and paired normal tissues from five deceased ESCC patients within a 5-year follow-up period from ESCC Cohort 1 at Huai’an First People’s Hospital Affiliated with Nanjing Medical University. 3

HPGD inhibits the malignant progression of ESCC cells
Although we established a link between HPGD expression and ESCC progression and patient outcomes, its functional role in ESCC cells remains unclear. To investigate the specific function of HPGD in ESCC cells, we evaluated HPGD expression in ESCC cell lines (Fig.
2
A–C), constructed a eukaryotic HPGD expression plasmid, and stably transfected the plasmid into ESCC cell lines presenting with low endogenous HPGD expression (Fig.
2
D–E). Real-time label-free cell proliferation assays revealed that HPGD significantly inhibited ESCC cell proliferation (Fig.
2
F–G), which was further confirmed by colony formation assays showing a significantly reduced proliferative capacity (Fig.
2
H–I). Soft agar colony formation assays demonstrated that HPGD inhibited anoikis resistance in ESCC cells, indicating reduced anchorage-independent growth potential (Fig.
2
J–L). Migration and invasion assays indicated that HPGD overexpression significantly reduced ESCC cell motility (Fig.
2
M–R). Furthermore, the results of annexin V staining and TUNEL assays indicated that HPGD promoted apoptosis in ESCC cells (Fig.
2
S–T). These results indicated that HPGD functions as a tumor suppressor in ESCC by inhibiting proliferation, migration, invasion, and anchorage-independent growth while promoting apoptosis.

HPGD overexpression affects the expression of genes involved in ferroptosis and autophagy in ESCC cells
To explore the role of HPGD in ESCC cells, we conducted RNA-seq and bioinformatics analyses of KYSE150 and KYSE30 cells that overexpressed HPGD. We found 530 and 727 differentially expressed genes in KYSE150 and KYSE30 cells, respectively (Fig.
3
A–D). GO analysis showed that these genes were enriched in cell homeostasis, structural stability, epithelial migration, and EMT (Fig.
3
E–F). KEGG analysis revealed effects on pathways such as cell cycle, ferroptosis, autophagy, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, AMPK, and cellular senescence (Fig.
3
G). Venn analysis of the differentially expressed genes from both cell Lines revealed 13 genes that were commonly dysregulated following HPGD overexpression, among which the TFRC gene was significantly upregulated (Fig.
3
H–I). The data revealed no significant changes in the expression levels of classical ferroptosis regulators, including ACSL4 and SLC7A11 (Supplementary Fig. 1A-B). Previous studies have shown that TFRC is involved in ferroptosis [
25
] and autophagosome formation [
26
]. Moreover, although autophagy can promote cellular survival during nutrient deprivation, excessive autophagy activation can lead to cell death, particularly autophagy-dependent ferroptosis [
27
,
28
]. These results suggest that HPGD may inhibit ESCC progression by modulating ferroptosis and autophagy pathways.

HPGD promoted TFRC expression by inhibiting ERK1/2 pathway activation through LXA4 degradation
To explore how HPGD affects TFRC expression in ESCC via ferroptosis and autophagy, we used a high-throughput protein phosphorylation array. We detected reduced ERK1/2 pathway activation and changes in P53 and RSK1/2 phosphorylation (Fig.
6
A). Western blotting analysis confirmed that HPGD overexpression decreased ERK1/2 phosphorylation without significantly affecting P53 or RSK1/2 phosphorylation (Fig.
6
B–C). Notably, the use of an ERK1/2 activator (EGF) reversed the effect of HPGD on ERK1/2 phosphorylation and reduced the levels of TFRC (Fig.
6
D–F). Previous studies have indicated that autophagy triggers ferroptosis by degrading ferritin and increasing TFRC levels [
32
]. However, our results revealed that blocking autophagy did not eliminate HPGD-induced TFRC upregulation, suggesting that HPGD does not increase autophagy to regulate the levels of TFRC (Fig.
6
G–H). HPGD serves as the principal catabolic enzyme for prostaglandins and LXA4. Prior research has demonstrated that LXA4 can activate the ERK‒Nrf2 signaling pathway, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and inhibiting apoptosis [
33
]. In the present study, we observed that the overexpression of HPGD led to a marked reduction in both the extracellular and intracellular concentrations of LXA4 (Fig.
6
I). The addition of LXA4 restored ERK1/2 signaling and reduced TFRC expression (Fig.
6
J–K). Thus, HPGD appears to upregulate TFRC by accelerating LXA4 degradation, which in turn leads to suppression of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway.

HPGD promotes the binding of RNA-binding protein (RBP) U2AF2 to the TFRC promoter, which improves its transcription by suppressing ERK1/2 signaling activation
To explore how the ERK1/2 signaling pathway regulates TFRC expression, we used a dual-luciferase reporter assay to identify the active region of the TFRC promoter (Fig.
7
A). Specific primers were used to amplify the TFRC promoter fragment, which was labeled with biotin and transfected into 293 T cells. After 48 h, DNA was extracted, sonicated, and subjected to a streptavidin pull-down assay to isolate promoter-bound proteins. These complexes were analyzed via SDS‒PAGE, and differentially bound proteins were identified using tandem mass spectrometry (Fig.
7
B). The analysis revealed 222 differentially bound proteins on the biotin-linked fragment with respect to a negative control fragment (Supplementary Material 1). On the basis of bioinformatics analysis and measured protein abundance, we selected the transcription factors SF3B1, TAF3, and YY1 and an RBP (i.e., U2AF2) for further validation by SDS‒PAGE (Fig.
7
C) and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) (Fig.
7
D). The ChIP results confirmed that U2AF2 specifically binds to the TFRC promoter in ESCC cells. We performed molecular docking to explore the U2AF2 protein’s interaction with the TFRC promoter using computational biology. The analysis showed U2AF2 likely binds the promoter through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions (Supplementary Fig. 3A-B). We mutated nucleotides in the promoter, inserted the mutated sequence into a pGL3 dual-luciferase reporter plasmid, and co-transfected it with a U2AF2 overexpression plasmid into 293 T cells. The results revealed a significant drop in luciferase activity (Fig.
7
E), confirming U2AF2’s direct binding to the TFRC promoter. Previous studies show that RBPs interact with RNA to regulate expression and affect tumor progression. To determine if U2AF2 directly interacts with TFRC mRNA, we conducted RNA-RIP experiments, which confirmed that U2AF2 does not bind to TFRC mRNA (Fig.
7
F).

HPGD facilitates ferroptosis in ESCC cells and concurrently promotes autophagy via the AMPK-mTOR signaling pathway
To verify that HPGD inhibits ESCC progression by promoting ferroptosis via TFRC upregulation, we assessed the intracellular iron concentration in ESCC cells presenting with HPGD overexpression with or without TFRC knockdown. HPGD overexpression significantly increased the level of intracellular iron, which was reversed by TFRC knockdown (Fig.
8
A). Excessive iron leads to Fenton reactions, generating ROS that cause lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. Consistent with this mechanism, upregulation of HPGD significantly increased the levels of intracellular ROS (Fig.
8
B) and both cellular and mitochondrial lipid peroxidation (Fig.
8
C–D). Key lipid peroxidation markers, such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and lipid hydroperoxides (LPO), were significantly increased, but TFRC knockdown reversed these effects (Fig.
8
E–F). Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which is dependent on glutathione (GSH), detoxifies lipid peroxides to prevent ferroptosis; inactivation or downregulation of GPX4 depletes GSH, weakening cellular defenses against oxidative stress and promoting ferroptosis. HPGD overexpression significantly reduced GSH levels and GPX4 activity, increasing the susceptibility of cells to ferroptosis, but TFRC knockdown reversed these effects (Fig.
8
G–H).

During ferroptosis, autophagy signaling is associated with oxidative stress and iron buildup. Normally, moderate ROS-induced autophagy reduces oxidative stress, preserves mitochondrial health, and protects cells. However, excessive ROS during ferroptosis can either activate or inhibit autophagy-related pathways such as AMPK [
29
] and mTOR [
30
], creating a feedback loop between ferroptosis and autophagy [
31
]. Our findings indicate that the overexpression of HPGD significantly increased autophagy, as shown by increased autophagic activity, AMPK pathway activation, and mTOR pathway suppression (Fig.
8
K–L). The increase in autophagy was negated by either TFRC knockdown or treatment with a ferroptosis inhibitor (Fig.
8
I–J). Additionally, TFRC upregulation alongside ROS scavenging reversed ferroptosis and autophagy activation, suppressed activity in the AMPK pathway, and reactivated the mTOR pathway (Fig.
8
M–O). To further elucidate the interrelationship between ferroptosis and autophagy, we employed an autophagy inhibitor to mitigate the hyperactivation of autophagy induced by HPGD overexpression. The results indicated that the inhibition of autophagy significantly reduced the levels of cellular ferroptosis (Supplementary Fig. 5A-G). Collectively, these findings suggest that in ESCC, HPGD can simultaneously induce both ferroptosis and autophagy, with these two processes engaging in a mutually reinforcing positive feedback loop.

9
A). The tumor growth curves and weights of the excised tumor tissues demonstrated that HPGD effectively inhibited tumor development (Fig.

Discussion
HPGD is a key enzyme involved in prostaglandin and LXA4 catabolism that negatively regulates the levels and activities of prostaglandins and LXA4 [
14
]. In addition, several reports have shown that HPGD can regulate mitochondrial function and autophagy, impede the signaling of transforming growth factors, and decrease the activity of the ubiquitin–proteasome system, thereby leading to antitumor activity [
23
]. However, its role in cancer, particularly in ESCC, remains inadequately understood.
Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, is linked to various diseases and can suppress tumor growth [
38
]. Tumor cells capture serum Fe³⁺ through transferrin (TF), which is recognized by the transferrin receptor (TFRC) on their surface. The TF–Fe³⁺ complex undergoes endocytosis, and Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ by STEAP3 and transported into the cytoplasm via DMT1 [
39
]. Studies have indicated that E3 ubiquitin ligases inhibit ferroptosis under liver conditions by degrading TFRC, while hypoxia-inducible factor-1α can counteract anthracycline resistance in breast cancer by increasing TFRC expression and activating ferroptosis [
40
]. This study revealed a strong connection between TFRC upregulation and ferroptosis. RNA-seq analysis revealed that genes associated with ferroptosis and autophagy pathways were significantly enriched in HPGD-overexpressing cells. While key regulators such as ACSL4 and SLC7A11 play critical roles in the regulation of classical ferroptosis [
37
], our study did not reveal any alterations in these established ferroptosis regulators. HPGD overexpression increased Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺ levels, but TFRC knockdown reversed this effect. Additionally, TFRC knockdown reversed the suppression of ESCC malignancy by HPGD, highlighting the role of TFRC in iron uptake and ferroptosis in the tumor-inhibiting effect of HPGD.
Within the cellular environment, Fe²⁺ can either move to mitochondria or stay in the cytoplasm. In the mitochondria, Fe²⁺ plays a critical role in facilitating oxygen consumption and the assembly of iron–sulfur clusters [
41
] and plays a crucial role in ferroptosis by regulating ATP synthesis, ROS production, and iron balance [
42
]. Typically, Fe²⁺ in the cytoplasm binds to ferritin, forming stable Fe³⁺ compounds. However, excess Fe²⁺ reacts with H₂O₂ via the Fenton reaction, generating ROS, which leads to lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis [
43
]. This reaction also produces hydroxyl radicals, causing damage to DNA, lipid membranes, and other biomolecules [
44
]. Our data revealed that HPGD-induced TFRC upregulation led to increased intracellular ROS levels, reduced glutathione (GSH) levels, and decreased GPx4 activity. GSH, a cofactor for GPx4, enables the enzyme to reduce lipid peroxides by converting their peroxide bonds into hydroxyl groups, thereby neutralizing their oxidative potential. A decrease in GSH impairs GPx4 function, resulting in the accumulation of lipid peroxides in ESCC. TFRC upregulation also increased the MDA and LPO levels in the cytoplasm and mitochondria. These effects were reversed upon TFRC knockdown. These results support the hypothesis that HPGD inhibits the malignant progression of ESCC cells by upregulating TFRC expression, thereby promoting ferroptosis.
The relationship between autophagy and ferroptosis is complex and context dependent, with both processes interacting in distinct ways under different conditions. A previous study indicated that autophagy promotes ferroptosis by increasing the sensitivity of cells to ferroptosis [
38
]. However, other study have shown contradictory results; for example, inhibiting autophagy in liver cancer cells led to the accumulation of lipid oxidation products [
45
]. These differences may result from heterogeneity in terms of cell types and variations in the tumor microenvironment. Recent research has highlighted the crucial role of iron accumulation-mediated ROS production in the induction of lipid peroxidation and the activation of autophagy during ferroptosis [
46
]. Specifically, erastin-induced ROS activate autophagy, promoting iron-dependent ferroptosis via ferritin degradation and TFRC upregulation [
47
]. Consistent with these findings, in this study, HPGD upregulated TFRC, causing excessive Fe
2+
accumulation and ROS production, which increased autophagy through AMPK‒mTOR signaling. After clearing the ROS generated by HPGD overexpression, AMPK pathway activity was suppressed, whereas mTOR activity was activated, resulting in autophagy inhibition. Interestingly, inhibition of HPGD-induced overactivation of autophagy may mitigate ferroptosis. Collectively, these findings indicate that HPGD plays a role in suppressing the progression of ESCC by modulating the positive feedback loop between ferroptosis and autophagy.
While previous studies have indicated that autophagy can induce TFRC expression, thereby leading to iron-dependent cell death, our findings demonstrate that the upregulation of TFRC following HPGD overexpression occurs independently of autophagic processes. Instead, we showed that TFRC expression was dependent upon the activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway, which is mediated by LXA4. In several models of inflammatory and oxidative stress-related diseases, LXA4 hinders ROS production, thereby reducing the negative effects of oxidative stress on cells [
48
]. Notably, recent cancer research has shown that LXA4 inhibits the FPRL1–ROS–NF-κB signaling pathway to suppress the paracrine release of Nodal in CAFs, thereby reducing the invasiveness and metastasis of gallbladder cancer [
49
]. Therefore, LXA4 may play an essential role in tumor progression. In this study, we revealed that the overexpression of HPGD, a crucial enzyme involved in LXA4 metabolism, led to a significant reduction in LXA4 levels in cells and culture supernatants, suggesting that HPGD facilitates LXA4 catabolism in ESCC cells. Importantly, the addition of exogenous LXA4 reversed the inhibition of ERK1/2 signaling pathway activation caused by HPGD overexpression, and the upregulation of TFRC was notably suppressed. Conversely, these effects were not replicated when autophagy inhibitors were applied.
Recent research has indicated that RBPs may function as transcription factors, engaging with gene promoters via traditional DNA binding mechanisms to modulate gene expression [
50
]. U2AF2 is an RNA-binding protein (RBP) and a pre-mRNA splicing factor that plays a pivotal regulatory role in RNA splicing [
51
]. Additionally, U2AF2 contributes to the stabilization of mRNA through binding interactions, thereby modulating gene expression [
52
,
53
]. Many studies have indicated that U2AF2 mutation and dysregulation are linked to cancer development. In melanoma, CD82 inhibits alternative CD44 splicing and reduces metastasis by promoting U2AF2 degradation [
54
]. In triple-negative breast cancer, U2AF2 enhances RPL23 translocation and c-Myc expression, increasing stemness [
55
]. In gliomas, U2AF2 stabilizes the circular RNA ARF1, activating the miR-342-3p–ISL2 axis and promoting angiogenesis [
56
]. In this study, we demonstrated that HPGD promoted U2AF2 binding to the TFRC promoter, thereby increasing the transcriptional activity of TFRC without affecting U2AF2 expression. Further investigation revealed that this binding depends on the ERK1/2 signaling pathway. Silencing U2AF2 via siRNA significantly reduced TFRC expression. A recent study on ESCC revealed that the RNA/DNA-binding protein TDP-43 could bind to the TP63 promoter in ESCC cells and promote TP63 expression [
35
]. Interestingly, our findings indicate that U2AF2 does not interact with the mRNA of TFRC to modulate its expression. Therefore, although U2AF2 is an RBP, it can also act as a transcription factor that regulates the transcriptional activity of TFRC. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that U2AF2 functions as a transcription factor that directly regulates gene transcriptional activity.
In summary, HPGD promotes LXA4 catabolism in ESCC cells, thereby inhibiting activation of the ERK1/2 signaling pathway. Inhibiting ERK1/2 activation facilitates the binding of the RBP U2AF2 to the TFRC promoter, which increases TFRC expression and drives ferroptosis in ESCC cells. ROS accumulation during ferroptosis further activates the AMPK–mTOR signaling pathway, which in turn stimulates autophagy.
